question: A bus driver must have a commercial driver license if the vehicle is designed to seat how many persons, including the driver?
choice_a: 8 or more
choice_b: 16 or more
choice_c: 12 or more
choice_d: 24 or more
explanation: The manual states that bus drivers must have a commercial driver license if they drive a vehicle designed to seat 16 or more persons, including the driver.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, Introduction

question: To obtain a passenger endorsement, a driver must pass a knowledge test covering which sections of the manual?
choice_a: Section 6, Combination Vehicles
choice_b: Sections 2 and 4 (and Section 5 if the bus has air brakes)
choice_c: Sections 1 and 3
choice_d: Only Section 4
explanation: To get the passenger endorsement, a driver must pass a knowledge test on Sections 2 and 4, and if the bus has air brakes, also on Section 5.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, Introduction

question: Before signing a previous driver's inspection report, what must a bus driver confirm?
choice_a: That the bus has a full tank of fuel
choice_b: That defects reported earlier have been certified as repaired or certified as not needing repair
choice_c: Nothing; the report can be signed without review
choice_d: That the previous driver has left the vehicle
explanation: A driver should only sign the previous driver's report if defects reported earlier have been certified as repaired or certified as not needing repair, since signing certifies the defects have been fixed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1 Vehicle Inspection

question: Which of the following is specifically noted about front wheel tires during a bus inspection?
choice_a: Front wheels must always have snow tires installed
choice_b: Front wheels must not have recapped or regrooved tires
choice_c: Front wheels are exempt from tire inspection
choice_d: Front tires must be replaced every 6 months
explanation: Among the vehicle systems checked before driving, the manual specifies that front wheels must not have recapped or regrooved tires.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.1 Vehicle Systems

question: As you check the outside of the bus before driving, what should you do with access panels and emergency exits?
choice_a: Close any open emergency exits and any open access panels
choice_b: Only close panels if it is raining
choice_c: Access panels do not need to be checked
choice_d: Leave all emergency exits open for ventilation
explanation: While checking the outside of the bus, the driver should close any open emergency exits and any open access panels (for baggage, restroom service, engine, etc.) before driving.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.2 Access Doors and Panels

question: Why does the manual say you should always check the interior of an unattended bus before driving?
choice_a: Because riders are required to inspect it themselves
choice_b: Because the interior is never inspected at the factory
choice_c: Because people sometimes damage unattended buses
choice_d: Interior checks are optional and rarely needed
explanation: The manual notes that people sometimes damage unattended buses, so the driver should always check the interior before driving to ensure rider safety.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.3 Bus Interior

question: Which statement about bus seats is accurate per the manual?
choice_a: Folding seats are exempt from fastening requirements
choice_b: Seats only need to be checked annually
choice_c: Only the driver's seat needs to be fastened
choice_d: All seats must be securely fastened to the bus
explanation: The manual states that the seats must be safe for riders, and all seats must be securely fastened to the bus.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.3 Bus Interior

question: Under what circumstance is it acceptable to drive a bus with an emergency exit door or window open?
choice_a: Never; you should never drive with an open emergency exit door or window
choice_b: When there are fewer than 10 riders aboard
choice_c: When the weather is warm
choice_d: When traveling under 30 mph
explanation: The manual is explicit: never drive with an open emergency exit door or window, and the Emergency Exit sign must be clearly visible.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.3 Bus Interior

question: When must the red emergency door light, if equipped, be turned on?
choice_a: Only when carrying more than 20 passengers
choice_b: It should always remain off unless the door is opened
choice_c: Only during a declared emergency
choice_d: At night or any other time the outside lights are used
explanation: If there is a red emergency door light, it must work and should be turned on at night or any other time the driver uses the outside lights.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.3 Bus Interior

question: What does the manual say about locking emergency roof hatches partly open?
choice_a: It may be done for fresh air, but should not be left open as a regular practice, and the driver must keep the bus's higher clearance in mind
choice_b: Roof hatches should always be left fully open in summer
choice_c: Roof hatches must remain fully closed and locked at all times while driving
choice_d: Roof hatches can only be opened when the bus is parked
explanation: Emergency roof hatches may be locked in a partly open position for fresh air, but should not be left open as a regular practice, and the driver should keep in mind the bus's higher clearance while driving with them open.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.4 Roof Hatches

question: If a bus is not equipped with circuit breakers, what must it have instead, according to the manual?
choice_a: A second set of headlights
choice_b: A backup battery pack
choice_c: An additional fire extinguisher
choice_d: Spare electrical fuses
explanation: The manual states the bus must have spare electrical fuses, unless it is equipped with circuit breakers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.4 Roof Hatches

question: What does the manual advise regarding the driver's seat belt on a bus?
choice_a: Only charter bus drivers need to wear seat belts
choice_b: The driver's seat should have a seat belt, and the driver should always use it for safety
choice_c: Seat belts are only required on buses with air brakes
choice_d: Seat belts are optional for bus drivers
explanation: The manual states the driver's seat should have a seat belt, and the driver should always use it for safety.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.1.5 Use Your Seatbelt

question: Why must carry-on baggage not be left in a doorway or aisle?
choice_a: Only because it looks unprofessional
choice_b: Baggage in the aisle is permitted as long as it is under 10 pounds
choice_c: Because it is against fire code in all states
choice_d: To allow the driver to move freely, allow riders to exit in an emergency, and protect riders from injury if items fall or shift
explanation: Secured baggage and freight should allow the driver to move freely and easily, allow riders to exit by any window or door in an emergency, and protect riders from injury if carry-ons fall or shift.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2 Loading and Trip Start

question: How many different diamond-shaped hazard labels does the Federal Hazardous Materials Table use to identify hazard classes?
choice_a: Twelve
choice_b: Four
choice_c: Six
choice_d: Nine
explanation: The manual states there are nine different four-inch, diamond-shaped hazard labels used to mark containers of hazardous material.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.1 Hazardous Materials

question: Which hazardous materials are buses permitted to carry, according to the manual?
choice_a: Tear gas and irritating materials
choice_b: Small-arms ammunition labeled ORM-D, emergency hospital supplies, and drugs
choice_c: Liquid Class 6 poisons in any quantity
choice_d: Labeled radioactive materials in the space occupied by riders
explanation: The manual states buses may carry small-arms ammunition labeled ORM-D, emergency hospital supplies, and drugs, and small amounts of certain other hazardous materials if the shipper has no other way to send them.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.2 Forbidden Hazardous Materials

question: What is the maximum amount of solid Class 6 poison a bus may ever carry?
choice_a: 500 pounds
choice_b: 100 pounds
choice_c: 50 pounds
choice_d: 250 pounds
explanation: The manual states buses must never carry more than 100 pounds of solid Class 6 poisons.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.2 Forbidden Hazardous Materials

question: What is the overall weight limit for allowed hazardous materials carried on a bus, and the per-class limit?
choice_a: No more than 1,000 pounds total, with no per-class limit
choice_b: There is no overall weight limit as long as materials are properly labeled
choice_c: No more than 250 pounds total, and no more than 50 pounds of any one class
choice_d: No more than 500 pounds total, and no more than 100 pounds of any one class
explanation: Buses must never carry more than 500 pounds total of allowed hazardous materials, and no more than 100 pounds of any one class.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.2 Forbidden Hazardous Materials

question: Besides small-arms ammunition, what other explosives may occupy the space where riders sit on a bus?
choice_a: Fireworks if properly labeled
choice_b: None; explosives are never allowed in the space occupied by people, except small-arms ammunition
choice_c: Dynamite in quantities under 10 pounds
choice_d: Any Class 1 explosive under 50 pounds
explanation: The manual states buses must never carry explosives in the space occupied by people, except small-arms ammunition.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.2 Forbidden Hazardous Materials

question: What is the "standee line" on a bus designed to allow standing riders?
choice_a: A boundary marking the maximum baggage storage area
choice_b: A painted line marking where the wheelchair lift deploys
choice_c: A two-inch line (or other marking) showing where standing riders may not stand, forward of the rear of the driver's seat
choice_d: A line indicating where fare payment must occur
explanation: No rider may stand forward of the rear of the driver's seat; buses that allow standing must have a two-inch line or similar marking, called the standee line, and standing riders must stay behind it.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.3 Standee Line

question: What should a driver announce when arriving at a destination or intermediate stop?
choice_a: The location, reason for stopping, next departure time, and bus number
choice_b: Only the bus number
choice_c: Nothing needs to be announced
choice_d: The driver's name and license number
explanation: The manual specifies announcing the location, reason for stopping, next departure time, and bus number at destinations or intermediate stops.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.4 At Your Destination

question: Why should charter bus drivers avoid allowing riders back on the bus before departure time?
choice_a: Because it is required by the standee line rule
choice_b: To reduce the weight of the bus during idling
choice_c: There is no specific reason given in the manual
choice_d: To help prevent theft or vandalism of the bus
explanation: The manual states charter bus drivers should not allow riders on the bus until departure time, as this will help prevent theft or vandalism of the bus.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.2.4 At Your Destination

question: When is the best time to mention rules about smoking, drinking, or use of radios/tape players on a charter or intercity trip?
choice_a: At the start of the trip
choice_b: Only after a violation occurs
choice_c: At the midpoint of the trip
choice_d: Rules should never be mentioned verbally
explanation: The manual advises mentioning rules about smoking, drinking, or use of radio and tape players at the start of the trip to help avoid trouble later.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.1 Passenger Supervision

question: What should a driver do before starting the bus after riders board or exit?
choice_a: Only wait if the rider is elderly
choice_b: Wait for them to sit down or brace themselves before starting
choice_c: Sound the horn and pull away
choice_d: Start moving immediately to stay on schedule
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to wait for riders to sit down or brace themselves before starting, and to make starts and stops as smooth as possible to avoid rider injury.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.2 At Stops

question: If a driver has a drunk or disruptive rider who needs to be discharged, where should this be done?
choice_a: Wherever is nearest, regardless of safety
choice_b: It may be safer at the next scheduled stop or a well-lighted area where there are other people
choice_c: The rider must be discharged immediately at the current location
choice_d: Only at the final destination
explanation: The manual states drivers must ensure a disruptive rider's safety and should not discharge them where it would be unsafe; it may be safer at the next scheduled stop or a well-lighted area with other people present.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.2 At Stops

question: Where do bus accidents often happen, according to the manual?
choice_a: Exclusively on rural roads
choice_b: Only in parking lots
choice_c: At intersections
choice_d: On straight highway sections
explanation: The manual states bus accidents often happen at intersections, and drivers should use caution even if a signal or stop sign controls other traffic.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.3 Common Accidents

question: If your bus leans toward the outside on a banked curve, what does this indicate?
choice_a: The tires are underinflated
choice_b: The curve's design speed is set too low
choice_c: The suspension needs replacement
choice_d: You are driving too fast
explanation: The manual states if your bus leans toward the outside on a banked curve, you are driving too fast, and drivers should reduce speed for curves.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.4 Speed on Curves

question: How far before a railroad crossing should a bus driver stop?
choice_a: Between 15 and 50 feet before the crossing
choice_b: Exactly 100 feet before the crossing
choice_c: Right at the crossing signal
choice_d: At least 200 feet before the crossing
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to stop between 15 and 50 feet before railroad crossings, listen and look both ways for trains.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.5 Railroad-highway Crossings Stops

question: If your bus has a manual transmission, what must you avoid doing while crossing railroad tracks?
choice_a: Applying the parking brake
choice_b: Changing gears
choice_c: Using the horn
choice_d: Using turn signals
explanation: The manual specifically warns that if your bus has a manual transmission, you should never change gears while crossing the tracks.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.5 Railroad-highway Crossings Stops

question: At which of the following is a bus driver NOT required to stop, but must instead slow down and carefully check for other vehicles?
choice_a: Any crossing with visible tracks
choice_b: A crossing marked as "exempt" or "abandoned"
choice_c: Any crossing near a school
choice_d: Every crossing regardless of markings
explanation: The manual lists crossings marked as "exempt" or "abandoned" (along with streetcar crossings, crossings directed by a flagman/police, or a green traffic signal) as situations where a stop is not required, but the driver must still slow down and check for other vehicles.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.5 Railroad-highway Crossings Stops

question: How far before a drawbridge without a signal light or traffic control attendant must a bus stop?
choice_a: At least 50 feet before the draw of the bridge
choice_b: At least 100 feet before the draw
choice_c: There is no required stopping distance
choice_d: At least 15 feet before the draw
explanation: The manual requires stopping at least 50 feet before the draw of a drawbridge that lacks a signal light or traffic control attendant, and confirming the draw is completely closed before crossing.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.6 Drawbridges

question: Under what condition can a bus driver approach a drawbridge without stopping, though still slowing down and checking that it is safe?
choice_a: Whenever traffic behind is heavy
choice_b: When there is a green traffic light, or an attendant/traffic officer controls traffic whenever the bridge opens
choice_c: Anytime the bridge is visible from a distance
choice_d: Bus drivers must always stop at every drawbridge with no exceptions
explanation: A driver does not need to stop, but must slow down and make sure it's safe, when there is a green traffic light or the bridge has an attendant/traffic officer who controls traffic whenever it opens.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.3.6 Drawbridges

question: What must an interstate carrier bus driver complete at the end of each shift?
choice_a: A fuel log only
choice_b: Nothing, unless a defect is found
choice_c: A verbal report to the next driver only
choice_d: A written inspection report specifying the bus and listing any defect affecting safety or that could cause a breakdown
explanation: If you work for an interstate carrier, you must complete a written inspection report for each bus driven, specifying the bus and listing any defect that would affect safety or result in a breakdown; if there are no defects, the report should say so.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.4 After-trip Vehicle Inspection

question: When, if ever, should a driver refuel a bus with riders on board?
choice_a: Only at night
choice_b: Avoid it unless absolutely necessary, and never refuel in a closed building with riders aboard
choice_c: It is always acceptable as long as the engine is off
choice_d: It is required practice at every fuel stop
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to avoid fueling a bus with riders on board unless absolutely necessary, and to never refuel in a closed building with riders on board.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.5 Prohibited Practices

question: Under what circumstance may a driver tow or push a disabled bus with riders still aboard?
choice_a: Only if getting off would be unsafe, and only to the nearest safe spot to discharge passengers
choice_b: Only on interstate highways
choice_c: This is always prohibited with no exceptions
choice_d: Whenever it saves time
explanation: The manual states drivers should not tow or push a disabled bus with riders aboard unless getting off would be unsafe, and even then only to the nearest safe spot to discharge passengers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.5 Prohibited Practices

question: What does a brake-door interlock system on an urban mass transit coach do?
choice_a: It disables the horn while the bus is in motion
choice_b: It applies the brakes and holds the throttle in idle position when the rear door is open, releasing when the door closes
choice_c: It automatically locks all doors when the parking brake is set
choice_d: It prevents the engine from starting until seat belts are fastened
explanation: The interlock applies the brakes and holds the throttle in idle position when the rear door is open, and releases when the driver closes the rear door.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.6 Use of Brake-door Interlocks

question: Should a driver rely on the brake-door interlock in place of the parking brake?
choice_a: Only during layovers under 5 minutes
choice_b: Only when parked on level ground
choice_c: Yes, it is designed as a full substitute for the parking brake
choice_d: No, the interlock should not be used in place of the parking brake
explanation: The manual explicitly warns not to use the brake-door interlock safety feature in place of the parking brake.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 4, Transporting Passengers Safely, 4.6 Use of Brake-door Interlocks
